You are allowed to close the tabs.

Being thoughtful about a decision doesn't mean researching until there's nothing left on the internet to read. You can spend hours gathering information and still feel uncertain about which direction to take.

Decision Untangler helps you move from collecting information to reflecting on what matters: https://decisionuntangler.garrettsdevdesk.com

Research becomes much more manageable when you give it a finish line.

Before comparing options, identify the facts that could genuinely change your choice. Maybe it's the total cost, a schedule requirement, or a risk you haven't investigated.

Once those questions have reasonable answers, you can stop searching for every possible detail. Being informed enough is a more practical goal than knowing everything.

Before reading another review or asking for another opinion, consider why you're still searching.

Are you missing information that could meaningfully change your decision? Or are you hoping someone will finally make one option feel completely safe?

That distinction matters. Decision Untangler helps you explore the concerns behind your uncertainty: https://decisionuntangler.garrettsdevdesk.com

Sometimes closing your browser is a useful part of making a decision.

When you're constantly reading other people's opinions, it can become difficult to recognize which concerns are actually yours. The loudest perspective isn't necessarily the most relevant to your life.

Try stepping away from outside input for a little while. Write down the thoughts that keep returning when nobody else is offering an answer.

Keeping every option open can have a cost of its own.

An unresolved decision may follow you through your workday, interrupt your evenings, and occupy weeks of mental energy. Sometimes the tradeoffs of choosing feel more intimidating than the ongoing cost of remaining undecided.

Decision Untangler helps you examine those tradeoffs and consider what moving forward might look like: https://decisionuntangler.garrettsdevdesk.com

Close the fifteen browser tabs. Make another cup of coffee. Give yourself a little room to think.

You may already know the important facts about your options. What you haven't had is enough quiet to consider what those facts mean for your priorities, responsibilities, and hopes.

When you're facing a difficult choice, does more research usually help you feel clearer, or does it sometimes make the decision harder?
